tagline: The deepest-living octopus, flapping on ear-like fins
summary: Dumbo octopuses are a genus of soft, jelly-like deep-sea octopuses named for the two ear-like fins above their eyes. They hover and 'hop' over the abyssal seafloor, and one was filmed nearly 7 km down, deeper than any other octopus or squid ever seen.

stats.size: Hadal individuals filmed at about 35–43 cm total length
stats.range: Probably worldwide in deep, cold water
stats.diet: Small seafloor animals: worms, copepods, amphipods, isopods
stats.conservation: Not evaluated by IUCN as a genus; most species are poorly known

facts.title: Deepest octopus on record
facts.text: In 2019 a baited camera lander in the Java Trench, Indian Ocean, filmed a Grimpoteuthis at 6,957 m: the first unequivocal sighting of any cephalopod in the hadal zone (below 6,000 m).

facts.title: Fins, not jets
facts.text: Unlike most octopuses, which jet water through a siphon, dumbos swim mainly by flapping their two fins, which helps them save energy in the food-poor deep sea.

facts.title: Hop, spread, repeat
facts.text: Filmed individuals foraged in short 'hops' across the mud, landing with arms and web spread before lifting off again. One picked up a tiny isopod, then dropped it.

facts.title: Eggs left on their own
facts.text: Dumbo octopuses attach large, tough-cased eggs to deep-sea corals and do not guard them. Hatchlings emerge as fully formed juveniles able to fend for themselves.

facts.title: A tangled family tree
facts.text: Telling species apart is hard: specimens are rare and often damaged, and many key features are internal, so photos alone rarely pin down a species.

references.title: First in situ observation of Cephalopoda at hadal depths (Octopoda: Opisthoteuthidae: Grimpoteuthis sp.) — Jamieson & Vecchione 2020

image.caption: A dumbo octopus (Grimpoteuthis) swims above the deep seafloor, filmed by NOAA's remotely operated vehicle; the scientists noted damage to an arm and fin

notes: WoRMS currently places Grimpoteuthis in family Grimpoteuthidae (the 2020 paper used Opisthoteuthidae). Both photos are NOAA Okeanos Explorer frames identified by NOAA only to genus (Grimpoteuthis); no Opisthoteuthis/other cirrate images used. Size given is from the two hadal individuals measured from video (350 and 430 mm total length), not a genus maximum. Commons 'Grimpoteuthis.jpg' (illustration) and G. bathynectes (1280 px) not used. Fin swimming, egg and diet facts are from Wikipedia (secondary; cites Collins & Villanueva 2006). Feeding has not been directly observed in Grimpoteuthis beyond the hadal isopod pick-up.
